questions.sub_skill: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups
questions.prompt: An NSG has two inbound rules: priority 100 deny TCP 3389 from Internet, priority 200 allow TCP 3389 from 203.0.113.0/24. An admin at 203.0.113.5 tries RDP. What happens?
options: Allowed: the more specific rule wins
Denied: rule 100 matches first and processing stops
Allowed: allow rules beat deny rules
Denied by DenyAllInBound at 65500
questions.explanation: Rules are processed from the lowest priority number, and processing stops at the first match. Give the allow rule a lower number than the deny rule.
why_not: NSGs don't pick the most specific rule; they stop at the first match by priority.
Allow and deny have no precedence; priority order decides.
Rule 100 matches before the default rule is reached.

questions.sub_skill: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups
questions.prompt: Web VMs are added and removed weekly. You need an NSG rule allowing HTTPS from the internet to whichever VMs are web servers, without editing the rule. What should you use?
options: A service tag of VirtualNetwork as the destination
One rule per VM private IP
A network security group on each NIC with priority 4096
An application security group as the rule's destination, with the web VMs' NICs as members
questions.explanation: ASGs group NICs by role, so rules follow membership rather than addresses.
why_not: That covers the whole network, not just web servers.
That needs rule changes every time a VM is added.
Per-NIC NSGs don't solve role-based targeting.

questions.sub_skill: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups
questions.prompt: Inbound traffic from the internet reaches a VM's subnet. The subnet NSG allows TCP 443, and the NIC has an NSG with no custom rules. Is the traffic allowed?
options: No; the NIC NSG's default DenyAllInBound blocks it, and inbound traffic must be allowed by both NSGs
Yes; the subnet NSG already allowed it
Yes; an NSG with no custom rules allows everything
No; NIC NSGs are evaluated before subnet NSGs for inbound
questions.explanation: Inbound traffic is evaluated by the subnet NSG and then the NIC NSG; a deny at either level blocks it.
why_not: When both levels have an NSG, both must allow the traffic.
Its default rules deny inbound internet traffic.
Inbound is evaluated subnet first, then NIC; the NIC's deny still applies.

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
questions.prompt: An administrator needs to know exactly which NSG rule is denying TCP 22 from 198.51.100.7 to a VM. Which tool answers that most directly?
options: Azure Advisor
The activity log
Network Watcher IP flow verify
Next hop
questions.explanation: IP flow verify tests a specific flow and reports whether it's allowed or denied, and which rule decided.
why_not: Advisor makes recommendations; it doesn't evaluate a specific packet.
It records management operations, not packet decisions.
Next hop reports routing, not security rule decisions.

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
questions.prompt: You need to see every security rule that applies to a VM's network interface, combining its subnet and NIC NSGs, with service tags expanded. Where do you look?
options: The subnet's NSG rules page
The VM's Activity log
Azure Policy compliance
The NIC's effective security rules
questions.explanation: Effective security rules show the aggregate of the NSGs applied to a network interface.
why_not: That shows only the subnet NSG.
It doesn't show rule evaluation.
Policy evaluates resource configuration, not traffic rules.

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
questions.prompt: Effective security rules for a VM's NIC show nothing. What is the most likely reason?
options: The NIC has no ASG membership
The VM isn't running
Service endpoints are disabled
Effective rules only show NIC-level NSGs
questions.explanation: Effective security rules are calculated for a running VM's network interface; start the VM to view them.
why_not: ASG membership doesn't affect whether effective rules are shown.
They're unrelated to effective rules.
They show subnet and NIC NSGs together.

questions.prompt: Developers need occasional SSH access to a single test VM, at no cost, without public IPs. What should you deploy?
options: Azure Bastion Developer SKU
Azure Bastion Basic SKU
A public IP on the VM with an NSG allowing SSH
Azure Bastion Premium SKU
questions.explanation: Bastion Developer is free, uses shared infrastructure, and connects to one VM at a time in supported regions.
why_not: Basic bills hourly and needs an AzureBastionSubnet and a public IP.
That exposes SSH to the internet.
Premium is the most expensive tier.

questions.prompt: Admins must connect through Bastion to VMs in three peered spoke VNets, using the native SSH client from their laptops. What is the minimum SKU?
options: Developer
Basic
Standard
Premium
questions.explanation: Connecting with the native client (az CLI) requires Standard or Premium; peering requires Basic or higher.
why_not: Developer doesn't support peered VNets or the native client.
Basic supports peering but not the native client.
Premium works, but Standard is the minimum for the native client.

questions.prompt: You deploy a dedicated Bastion host. Which subnet configuration is required?
options: Any subnet /29 or larger
A subnet named BastionSubnet, /24
No subnet; Bastion is fully shared
A subnet named AzureBastionSubnet, /26 or larger
questions.explanation: Basic, Standard and Premium need a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet with a prefix of /26 or larger.
why_not: Dedicated SKUs need the specific name and at least /26.
The name must be exactly AzureBastionSubnet.
That's only the Developer SKU.

questions.sub_skill: Configure service endpoints for Azure platform as a service (PaaS)
questions.prompt: A storage account must accept traffic only from subnet App in VNet1, at no extra cost. What should you configure?
options: A private endpoint in subnet App
A Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on subnet App, and a virtual network rule for App on the storage firewall
An NSG on subnet App allowing Storage
An ASG containing the storage account
questions.explanation: Service endpoints are free; combined with a VNet rule on the storage firewall, they restrict the account to the subnet.
why_not: That works but bills hourly; the requirement is no extra cost.
An NSG controls the VNet side, not who the storage account accepts.
ASGs contain NICs, not PaaS services.

questions.sub_skill: Configure service endpoints for Azure platform as a service (PaaS)
questions.prompt: After enabling a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on a subnet, what does a VM in that subnet see when it resolves mystorage.blob.core.windows.net?
options: The same public IP address as before
A private 10.x address from the subnet
No answer, because public resolution is disabled
The VM's own private IP
questions.explanation: A service endpoint changes the source address used to reach the service, not the destination; DNS still returns the public endpoint.
why_not: That's what a private endpoint with private DNS does.
Service endpoints don't change DNS.
DNS for the service doesn't change to the VM's address.

questions.sub_skill: Configure service endpoints for Azure platform as a service (PaaS)
questions.prompt: On-premises servers connected over VPN must reach a storage account that's restricted with a service endpoint. Why does it fail?
options: The VPN gateway must also have a service endpoint
Service endpoints only work in the same region as the VNet
The storage account needs a stored access policy
Service endpoints don't extend to on-premises networks; the account isn't reachable from there unless you allow on-premises public IPs or use a private endpoint
questions.explanation: By default, resources secured to VNets with service endpoints aren't reachable from on-premises. Use a private endpoint for private on-premises access.
why_not: Gateways can't use subnet service endpoints this way.
Storage service endpoints work across regions; on-premises is the issue.
Stored access policies govern SAS tokens, not network access.

questions.sub_skill: Configure private endpoints for Azure PaaS
questions.prompt: A storage account must be reached privately from a VNet and from on-premises over ExpressRoute, and its public endpoint must be disabled. What should you deploy?
options: A service endpoint and a VNet firewall rule
Bastion Standard
A private endpoint for the account, integrated with a private DNS zone, then disable public network access
A route table sending Storage traffic to the gateway
questions.explanation: Private endpoints give the resource a private IP reachable from peered and on-premises networks, and allow disabling public access.
why_not: Service endpoints don't support on-premises access and keep the public endpoint.
Bastion provides RDP and SSH to VMs, not PaaS access.
Routing doesn't give the account a private address.

questions.sub_skill: Configure private endpoints for Azure PaaS
questions.prompt: A private endpoint for a storage account exists, but applications still connect to its public IP. What is the most likely cause?
options: DNS: the privatelink private DNS zone isn't linked to the VNet, or the clients' DNS doesn't resolve it
The private endpoint needs a public IP
Service endpoints must also be enabled
The NSG on the endpoint subnet blocks DNS
questions.explanation: Clients use the normal name; it must resolve via the private DNS zone to the private IP for traffic to use the endpoint.
why_not: Private endpoints don't use public IPs.
They're unnecessary for a private endpoint.
The symptom is resolution to the public IP, a DNS configuration issue.

questions.sub_skill: Configure private endpoints for Azure PaaS
questions.prompt: Security requires that compromised VMs can't copy data to storage accounts outside the organization, even over the Microsoft backbone. Which approach gives instance-scoped access?
options: Service endpoints for Microsoft.Storage
Private endpoints for the approved accounts
An NSG allowing the Storage service tag
Bastion Premium session recording
questions.explanation: Private endpoints map to a specific resource instance, which provides built-in protection against data exfiltration.
why_not: Service endpoints apply to the whole service, including other customers' accounts.
The service tag covers all storage, not your accounts only.
Recording covers admin sessions, not data paths.
